lesson.title: The Same Amount of Scatter, All the Way Across
lesson.summary: The equal variance condition requires that the spread of residuals stay roughly constant across the full range of x, rather than fanning out or squeezing in as x changes.
lesson.body:
The equal variance condition, also called homoscedasticity, requires that the spread of the residuals stays roughly consistent across the entire range of x, rather than fanning wider or squeezing narrower as x changes. This matters because the SE(b1) formula uses one single number, s, the residual standard deviation, to summarize 'typical leftover scatter' for the whole dataset at once. That single number only tells an honest story if the scatter really is roughly the same size everywhere. If residuals are tightly packed for small x and widely scattered for large x (or the reverse), no single s can honestly describe both regions, and the standard error, t-statistic, and confidence interval built from that s become less trustworthy.

The way to check is the same residual plot used for linearity, but looking for a different pattern: instead of curvature, look for the vertical band of residuals changing width as x increases, fanning out into a cone or funnel shape rather than staying an even band.

A realistic (if qualitative) example: imagine modeling a household's annual entertainment spending from its annual income across a wide range of incomes. Low-income households have little discretionary money, so their entertainment spending clusters tightly near a small value. High-income households have vastly more discretionary money, and how much of it goes toward entertainment varies enormously from one family to the next, some spend heavily, others barely at all. A residual plot for data like that would fan outward as income rises: a tight band of residuals on the left, a wide spray on the right, a textbook case of unequal variance.

Checking the six residuals from the hours-studied example against x = 1 through 6, 0, 0.2, −0.6, 0.6, −0.2, 0, there's no obvious funnel shape; if anything, the two largest-magnitude residuals (−0.6 and 0.6) sit in the middle of the x-range rather than concentrated at one end, which is mildly reassuring, again with the caveat that six points make any such pattern hard to judge with real confidence.

Unequal variance doesn't bias the slope estimate itself, the least-squares line still comes out the same, but it does bias the standard error, typically making it look smaller than it should, which in turn makes p-values look smaller and confidence intervals look narrower than they honestly are. Fixing it, through transforming y or using weighted regression, is beyond this course, but recognizing the fan shape in a residual plot is the key diagnostic skill.
